strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: applying outcome-based online RL to open-ended long-form writing, where verifiable rewards are unavailable; this is a relevant and timely direction for the community.

The framework is coherent and well-motivated: Margin-aware Data Selection (learning potential rather than difficulty), Pairwise Comparison Reward against graded references, and Dynamic Reference Scheduling together form a sensible curriculum design aligned with recent insights about 'not too easy, not too hard' samples in RL.

Comprehensive ablation studies: the paper systematically isolates each component (data selection strategies in Table 3, reward design in Table 4, reference quality in Table 5, and curriculum scheduling in Table 6), which strengthens the causal claims about what drives the gains.

The observation that long-output RL generalizes to long-input reasoning (Table 2), while SFT degrades, is an interesting and potentially impactful finding for long-context training research, and the paper is appropriately cautious in interpreting it.

Reasonable evaluation hygiene: three established benchmarks, diverse judges different from the training judge, prompts and training hyperparameters provided in the appendix, and a stated intention to release code.
Writing quality and structure are generally clear; Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 make the scheduling mechanism concrete.
weaknesses: The entire training signal depends on an LLM judge (Qwen-Plus) whose reliability, calibration, and hackability for long-form pairwise comparisons are not validated. The paper acknowledges position bias and uses a positional-disadvantage heuristic, but provides no measurement of judge agreement with humans on the training distribution, no analysis of reward variance over training, and no check for reward hacking (e.g., whether the policy degenerates into judge-pleasing styles). This weakens the central claim that quality genuinely improved rather than judge preference was gamed.

No human evaluation anywhere in the paper, despite LLM-judge evaluation of creative writing being known to be unreliable (the paper itself cites position and self-enhancement bias in Section 2). All headline numbers rest on LLM judges.

Reproducibility is limited: reference generation and judging rely on closed-source APIs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, Qwen-Plus, DeepSeek R1), and the 'Code is released at' statement is empty. A third party could only approximately reproduce the results.

Generalization claims (Section 5) rest on small gains (29.6→31.8, 30.2→32.8) on a single benchmark with two models, no variance estimates or significance testing, and only post-hoc intuitive explanations; the conclusion 'training on long-output tasks may enhance long-input reasoning' is stated too strongly given the evidence.

Editorial sloppiness that undermines confidence: cross-references are broken (Section 6.4 refers to 'Table 3.3' instead of Table 6, twice), the text reports Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL average as 87.14 while Table 1 shows 87.40, and duplicated paragraphs appear in Section 6.4.

Novelty of the individual components is moderate: pairwise rewards against model-generated references, margin-based data selection, and curriculum scheduling are all well-established ideas combined here; the contribution is primarily empirical engineering rather than a new methodological insight, and there is limited analysis of why the combination works (e.g., reward dynamics, win-rate curves over references).

Some baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: Suri-7B and LongWriter-9B use different base models and training recipes, and the SFT baselines were trained by the authors on one dataset (WritingBench), making the 'SOTA 7B writer' claim partially a function of baseline choices rather than a like-for-like comparison.
Ablations are run on a single dataset/model combination (Qwen2.5-7B on WritingBench Hard), so the component-wise conclusions may not transfer to the other training setup (LongWriter, Llama).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored problem: applying online outcome-based RL to long-form writing where verifiable rewards are unavailable. The framing of the three challenges (data selection, reward design, curriculum scheduling) is clear and well-motivated.

The proposed framework is coherent and each component is individually motivated: margin-aware data selection (learning potential rather than difficulty), pairwise comparison reward against graded references, and dynamic per-sample reference promotion (Algorithm 1 is clearly specified).

The ablation study is reasonably thorough: each of the three components is ablated separately (Tables 3-6), including comparisons against difficulty-prioritized selection, pointwise rewards, static reference sets of varying quality, and none/static/dynamic curricula. The observation that reference quality has a non-monotonic effect on training (self-generated saturates; best-reference starves positive rewards) is an interesting and useful empirical finding.

Training details (VeRL, PPO hyperparameters, hardware, prompt templates for judges and benchmarks) are documented in the appendix, and evaluation judges differ from the reward judge, showing some awareness of judge-overfitting risks.

The LongBench v2 experiment is a thoughtful probe of a genuinely interesting question (does long-output RL transfer to long-input reasoning?), with a length-distribution analysis (Figure 3) supporting the claim that training lengths do not cover evaluation lengths.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is the central concern. All three writing benchmarks are scored by LLM judges, and the reward signal during training is also an LLM judge (Qwen-Plus) with prompts adapted from the same family of templates as WritingBench. Moreover, the models are trained on the WritingBench training set and evaluated on WritingBench with the WritingBench critic model. Even though the paper argues judges differ, the risk of optimizing toward judge-preferred stylistic features (length, rubric-following) rather than genuine writing quality is not ruled out. There is no human evaluation anywhere in the paper, which is a significant omission for a paper whose headline claim is improved writing quality.

The headline 'surprising generalization' from long-output RL to long-input reasoning rests on small gains (29.6 to 31.8 and 30.2 to 32.8 on LongBench v2) with no variance estimates, significance tests, or multiple seeds. The causal explanation offered ('long-generation requires long-input understanding') is purely intuitive, and the paper itself acknowledges the systematic exploration is left to future work. The claim is arguably over-claimed relative to the evidence.

Reproducibility is limited: the pipeline depends on closed-source models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, Qwen-Plus, DeepSeek-R1) for reference generation and grading, the judge model is a fine-tuned critic whose training details are inherited from another paper, and the code release link is empty in the submitted PDF ('Code is released at' with no URL).

Polish and consistency problems undermine confidence: Section 6.4 repeatedly cites 'Table 3.3,' which does not exist (the intended table is Table 6); the criteria prompt box in Appendix A.1 contains a literal 'criteria' placeholder; several grammatical errors ('there exists several bias of including position bias'); and 'Code is released at' is unfinished. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Several design choices are asserted rather than validated. The claim that deliberately placing the model response in the disfavored second position 'imposes additional learning pressure' and halves cost is not ablated, and systematic positional disadvantage could instead teach reward hacking behaviors; no analysis is provided. Similarly, the tie reward of 0.5 and the promotion rule (promote on any single win) are not examined for sensitivity.

Ablations are conducted in a single narrow setting (Qwen2.5-7B on WritingBench Hard, judged only on WritingBench), and reported as single-point scores without error bars, so the relative rankings of data selection strategies (86.40 vs 87.02) and curricula (83.87 vs 84.49) may not be robust.

The base SFT models are already very strong (81.98-84.25 average), so the marginal contribution of the RL framework over simply continuing SFT with more teacher data is shown on only one comparison (12k vs 24k SFT), and the 'data saturation' argument is qualitative.

strengths: Addresses a timely and genuinely under-explored problem: applying online outcome-based RL to long-form writing, where verifiable rewards are absent. The framing of the three challenges (data selection, reward design, curriculum scheduling) is clear and well-motivated.

The Dynamic Reference Scheduling mechanism is a sensible and somewhat novel curriculum idea for open-ended generation: per-sample asynchronous promotion to stronger references when the policy surpasses the current one, avoiding both reward sparsity (too-strong references) and saturation (too-weak references), as supported by the analysis in Section 6.3.

Each proposed component is supported by an ablation (Tables 3-6): margin-aware vs. difficulty-prioritized data selection, pairwise vs. pointwise reward, reference quality, and static vs. dynamic curriculum, which strengthens the empirical case beyond a single headline number.

The observation that long-output RL training improves long-input reasoning (Table 2) while SFT hurts it is an interesting, potentially impactful finding, with a plausible discussion of why RL might generalize better than SFT.

Good transparency for reproducibility: implementation details (VeRL, PPO hyperparameters, hardware), full judge prompt templates for both data selection and evaluation, and a code release promise. Evaluation judges are deliberately chosen to differ from the reward judge, partially mitigating judge-overfitting concerns.
The paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with a related-work section that correctly positions the contribution against curriculum-RL and long-form-writing literature.
weaknesses: All central claims rest on LLM-as-Judge scores with no human evaluation. Given that the reward signal itself is an LLM judge and the paper itself acknowledges judge biases (position bias, self-enhancement bias), the absence of any human verification of the writing-quality gains is a significant soundness gap: RL may be optimizing judge-preferred surface features rather than genuine writing quality.

The 'positional disadvantage' trick (always placing the model response second) is claimed to impose useful learning pressure, but it also means the learned reward partly encodes the judge's position bias rather than quality. There is no experiment measuring win rates under swapped positions or judge robustness, so the semantics of the reward are not validated.

Statistical rigor is weak: results are single training runs with no variance estimates or significance tests, and gains over strong SFT baselines are moderate (e.g., 84.49 vs. 81.98 average for Qwen2.5; ~2-point LongBench v2 differences), making the 'SOTA' and 'surprising generalization' claims harder to assess.

The generalization finding is overclaimed relative to the evidence: LongBench v2 improvements over SFT are small and mixed across length buckets (e.g., Long: 26.5 vs. 20.4 for Qwen but 24.1 vs. 24.1 for Llama), and the mechanistic explanation is intuitive speculation rather than analysis.

Baseline fairness is unclear: RL is applied on top of an SFT model trained on the full WritingBench set, and the selected 1.5k RL samples derive from the same distributions; a direct comparison against simple rejection sampling or best-of-n distillation from the same reference pool is missing, which would isolate the benefit of online RL.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on closed-source models (Qwen-Plus as reward judge, GPT-4o/Claude-3.7/DeepSeek-R1 as reference generators); the training signal cannot be exactly reproduced, and judge model updates could change results.

Editing/presentation errors undermine polish: Section 6.4 contains a duplicated paragraph and refers to 'Table 3.3' (nonexistent; should be Table 6), and the text reports Llama3.1-8B average 87.14 while Table 1 shows 87.40.

Some method details are underspecified for faithful reproduction: how many reference-quality tiers per sample, the top-k selection threshold sensitivity, how ties (0.5 reward) are distributed, and how reference promotion interacts with batch-level rewards.

strengths: The three-component framework (margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, dynamic reference scheduling) is coherently motivated, and the dynamic per-sample reference promotion (Algorithm 1) is a genuinely neat mechanism for curriculum RL in non-verifiable domains.

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: results across three model families (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama3.1-8B), three writing benchmarks, component-wise ablations (Tables 3–5), judge-model ablations (Table 7), RL-algorithm robustness (PPO vs GRPO), sample-size ablation, general-capability checks (MT-Bench/MMLU), human evaluation, and a detailed cost analysis supporting reproducibility.

The output-to-input generalization finding is intriguing and handled responsibly: the paper provides length-distribution analysis, contamination checks (exact match, topic overlap, task-format differences), controlled SFT-vs-RL ablations, and failure-mode analysis rather than just asserting the phenomenon.

The Reference-SFT baselines (SFT on the same RL references) are a well-chosen control that directly supports the SFT data-saturation argument; improvements over both WritingBench-SFT and Reference-SFT baselines are consistent across families and reported with standard deviations from multiple runs.

Human judge agreement study (300 samples, 5 annotators, Cohen's kappa 0.69) and a rationale for the training judge choice strengthen confidence in the reward signal; evaluation judges are kept distinct from the training judge to reduce reward-model overfitting.
weaknesses: The method is effectively distilling the quality of proprietary teacher LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Plus) into the policy. The claimed ability to go 'beyond the SFT ceiling' is not tested against the teacher models themselves; comparisons to the reference-generating LLMs (e.g., Qwen-Plus scores) would clarify whether RL genuinely exceeds the teacher signal.

The pairwise reward design embeds several ad hoc heuristics that are only partially validated: always placing the model response in the disadvantageous second position (halving judge calls but confounding positional-bias compensation with a fixed difficulty knob), and the 0.5 tie reward, which may cause reward saturation; no analysis of tie rates or win-rate dynamics over training is provided.

Evaluation remains LLM-as-judge-centric, which is especially delicate for open-ended writing where the paper itself acknowledges judge biases. Human evaluation covers only 100 instructions with a single binary preference judgment per pair; gains of ~2 points over Reference-SFT are modest relative to the reported variance of LLM-judge scoring.

The generalization claim, while the most novel observation, is underpowered: the LongBench v2 gain is ~2–3 points and the mechanistic explanation (long-output training requires long-input understanding) is speculative; the case study of one sample cannot establish why RL but not SFT transfers.

Novelty is incremental: each component combines known ingredients (LLM-as-judge pairwise rewards from RLHF practice, curriculum/difficulty-based sample selection from recent reasoning-RL work); the strongest contribution is the dynamic reference scheduling, and its benefit over static scheduling (84.49 vs 83.83) is small though consistent.

Minor presentation and consistency issues: an incomplete code-release footnote undermines reproducibility claims; small numerical inconsistencies across tables (e.g., Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL average 87.29 in Table 1 vs 87.40 in Table 17; identical LongBench-Write scores for 'None' and 'Static' in Table 5); some ablation narratives (e.g., Table 8's 'Best Reference' result) are confusingly presented.

The position-disadvantage trick interacts with known judge position bias in a way that could be gamed (optimizing for judge preferences under a specific ordering) rather than improving true writing quality; sensitivity to judge ordering/prompt variants is not analyzed.

strengths: The proposed framework is clearly articulated: margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, and dynamic reference scheduling are well-motivated, and Algorithm 1 makes the per-sample asynchronous curriculum concrete and implementable.

The evaluation effort is above average for this line of work: multiple benchmarks (WritingBench, LongBench-Write, Creative-Writing-Bench), three independent runs with variance reported, human pairwise evaluation, and ablations over data selection, reward design, curriculum scheduling, judge model, reference quality, and sample size.

The paper provides a detailed and honest cost/reproducibility analysis (API fees, GPU hours per stage), a released-code statement, and an explicit limitations section, including discussion of the zero-RL regime.

The output-to-input generalization observation is potentially interesting, and the paper takes it seriously enough to run controlled ablations (SFT on RL data vs. RL), contamination checks (length distribution, task format, exact-match), and qualitative case studies.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity and judge dependence undermine the headline claims. The data-selection grading and WritingBench evaluation use the same fine-tuned critic/prompt pipeline (Appendix A.1/B), and the training reward judge is itself an LLM trained/aligned by a related lab. Even with the DeepSeek-V3 judge ablation, all reported writing gains (~1-2.5 points over strong SFT) are LLM-judge scores on benchmarks whose criteria were partly co-designed with the training signal; the human evaluation (100 samples, win-rate figure only) is too small to be decisive.

The reported gains are modest and internally inconsistent. Table 1 reports Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL average 87.29 (LongBench-Write 92.09), while Table 17 reports 87.40 (92.36); the differences between PPO and GRPO, and between SFT baselines (82.00 vs 82.17), are within the reported standard deviations, yet are narrated as meaningful. No significance testing is provided anywhere.

The output-to-input generalization claim — arguably the paper's most novel contribution — rests on a delta of 29.6 → 31.8 on LongBench v2 across only two model families, with no confidence intervals and a plausible confound: the RL model simply produces longer, reasoning-style outputs (Table 14), and a 100%-creative-only training set cannot support the strong causal narrative in Section 5. The 'explanation' in Section 5 is speculation, not evidence.

The core technical contributions are incremental. Margin-aware selection is a direct adaptation of difficulty filtering (Bae et al., Shi et al.) with scores substituted for accuracy; pairwise reward against references is standard RLHF-style LLM-judge reward; dynamic reference scheduling is a straightforward curriculum variant. The paper does not clearly delineate what is new versus recombined.

Design choices are justified post hoc rather than validated. Deliberately placing the model response in the positionally disadvantaged slot 'to impose additional learning pressure' is asserted, not ablated; the reward uses a single judge call per rollout with no position-swap control, so reward noise and length/style biases of the judge are unquantified.

Reproducibility depends heavily on closed-source APIs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Plus) for reference generation, grading, and reward; results will drift as these models update, and the paper offers no way to reproduce the reference set or judge exactly.

Writing quality issues and sloppy cross-references (e.g., 'the results are shown in 17', inconsistent capitalization, minor typos like 'cotexts', 'capablities') and missing human-evaluation details (number of annotators, agreement for the Fig. 2 study) reduce polish and trust.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: adaptive online RL for open-ended long-form writing, where verifiable rewards are unavailable. The framing of the three challenges (data selection, reward design, curriculum scheduling) is clear and well-motivated.

The framework is technically coherent. Margin-aware Data Selection (learning potential as a gap between policy and best competitor) is a sensible adaptation of difficulty-based selection to the non-verifiable setting, and Dynamic Reference Scheduling is a clean, sample-level asynchronous curriculum mechanism that avoids the extra-rollout overhead of prior adaptive-selection methods (Algorithm 1 is easy to follow and implement).

The experimental program is unusually thorough for this area: three model families (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama3.1-8B), three writing benchmarks plus LongBench v2, GRPO/PPO robustness check, ablations of every component (data selection, reward design, curriculum, judge model, reference quality, sample size), human evaluation with a proper agreement study (300 samples, 5 annotators, Cohen's kappa reported), and a full cost breakdown that supports reproducibility claims.

The evaluation design shows good awareness of judge-related pitfalls: training-time judges differ from evaluation-time judges, judge-model ablation (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-OSS-120B) is included, and pairwise comparisons deliberately place model responses in the disadvantaged second position.

The output-to-input generalization finding is interesting and handled responsibly: the paper distinguishes it from the headline contribution, backs it with controlled ablations (SFT-on-RL-data vs. RL), contamination analysis (length distribution, task format, exact-match checks), failure modes, and a case study with reasoning traces, and frames it cautiously as motivation for future work rather than an established result.
Honest reporting of negative/contextual results (SFT data saturation, Reference-SFT showing no gain or slight degradation) and a substantive Limitations section (model scale, RL-zero setup).
weaknesses: The headline writing gains are modest: roughly +2 to +3.5 average points over a strong WritingBench-SFT baseline, and the SFT data-scaling curve itself is nearly flat (82.17 vs. 82.00), so a portion of the apparent improvement could reflect run-to-run variance even with three evaluation runs; no statistical significance testing is reported despite std. deviations being shown.

Training and evaluation both depend on LLM judges, an acknowledged reliability risk. The mitigation (different judges at train vs. test time, agreement of 0.75) is reasonable but imperfect: 0.75 agreement with humans, and judge-dependent biases (position, length, style preferences) could still shape both the reward signal and the measured gains in ways the ablations only partially rule out.

Possible train/test proximity in writing evaluation: models are SFT'd on the WritingBench training set and evaluated on WritingBench (and RL data is derived from LongWriter training data, evaluated on LongBench-Write from the same authors/lineage). The contamination analysis in Appendix C addresses LongBench v2, but not the writing benchmarks; a statement on overlap between training sets and writing test sets is needed.

Novelty is incremental: the work is primarily a well-engineered combination of known ingredients (curriculum RL, pairwise LLM-judge rewards, margin/difficulty-based data filtering) adapted to writing; Dynamic Reference Scheduling is the most distinctive piece but is conceptually close to existing adaptive-difficulty RL (Bae et al., Shi et al.) with quality-ranked references substituted for correctness.

The generalization claim, while intriguing, is small in magnitude (+2 to +3 points on LongBench v2 MCQA) and the mechanistic explanation (long-output training builds long-input understanding) is largely speculative; one case study of a self-correction trace is suggestive but not conclusive evidence for the causal story.

Reproducibility gaps: the code release link in the paper appears empty/unfilled, and the proprietary reference/judge models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Plus) mean the training signal is not fully replicable even with released data and code; several human-evaluation details (number of annotators for the main evaluation in Fig. 2) are underspecified.

Minor presentation issues: some appendix table/cross-references are confusing (e.g., reference to 'Table 17' without table notation in D.4, inconsistent capitalization in later sections), and Table 1 mixes heterogeneous baselines (Suri-7B, Longwriter-9B) whose training data and judge protocols differ, complicating direct comparability.
